questions.q: Why can't qualities like 'is this response actually helpful' or 'does this writing sound natural' be reduced to an automated benchmark score?
options: They can always be measured automatically with perfect accuracy
They require judgment informed by context, domain knowledge, or taste that current automated metrics don't reliably capture, which is why human evaluation is reserved for them
These qualities don't matter for evaluating language models
Automated scores are always more accurate than human judgment for every quality
questions.explain: These qualities require contextual or domain judgment that automated metrics can't reliably capture, which is exactly why human evaluation exists as a complement to benchmarks rather than a replacement for them.

questions.q: Why is pairwise comparison often easier and more consistent for annotators than independently rating a single output?
options: Because judging relative quality between two options is a simpler cognitive task than assigning an absolute score to one output in isolation
Because pairwise comparison never requires any human judgment at all
Because pairwise comparison always produces a tie
Because it eliminates the need for any rubric whatsoever
questions.explain: Judging which of two outputs is better is a simpler relative task than assigning an absolute numeric score, making pairwise comparison generally more consistent across annotators.

questions.q: Why does a detailed rubric improve on simply asking annotators to 'rate the quality' of a response?
options: A rubric makes the criteria explicit and shared, preventing annotators from silently applying different, unstated criteria that reduce consistency
Rubrics are not actually helpful and add unnecessary complexity
A rubric eliminates the need to check inter-annotator agreement afterward
Rubrics are only useful for benchmark-based evaluation, not human evaluation
questions.explain: An explicit, shared rubric prevents the inconsistency that arises when different annotators weight unstated criteria (like correctness vs. tone) differently when asked for an open-ended quality judgment.

questions.q: What does inter-annotator agreement, as measured by Cohen's or Fleiss' kappa, actually tell you?
options: The exact number of annotators required for any evaluation task
Whether independent annotators reach the same judgment on the same items, correcting for the agreement expected by pure chance -- low agreement means the average score is effectively noise
The total cost in dollars of running the human evaluation
The benchmark score the model would achieve on MMLU
questions.explain: Kappa statistics measure whether annotators actually agree beyond what chance would predict; low kappa signals that the rubric or task is ambiguous and that aggregated scores aren't trustworthy.

questions.q: Why might a production evaluation setup use both pairwise comparison and Likert-scale rating rather than just one?
options: Because pairwise comparison and Likert rating always produce identical results
Pairwise comparison suits head-to-head checkpoint decisions, while Likert ratings provide an absolute score useful for tracking quality over time -- the two serve different purposes
Because using both methods is required by law for any AI evaluation
Because Likert ratings cannot be used to compare two different models at all
questions.explain: Pairwise comparison directly answers relative questions (is the new checkpoint better?), while Likert ratings give an absolute score that can be tracked over time -- different evaluation needs each design serves well.
